h1: California HOA Harassment by Board Member Demand Letter
metaTitle: California HOA Board Harassment Demand Letter
metaDescription: Stop HOA board member harassment in California. Generate a powerful demand letter citing the Davis-Stirling Act and protect your rights as a homeowner today.
statuteCitation: California Civil Code §§ 4000-6150 (Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act); Civil Code § 5975; Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6
deadline: 30 days to respond under IDR; 90 days for ADR request
penalty: Injunctive relief, civil penalties of up to $500 per violation under certain Davis-Stirling provisions (for example Civil Code § 4515(d)), attorney's fees under Civil Code § 5975(c) if you prevail in an action to enforce the governing documents, and civil harassment restraining orders
introParagraph: If you live in a California HOA and a board member is targeting you with intimidation, retaliation, selective enforcement, or personal attacks, you have strong legal protections. California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act sets strict rules on how board members must conduct themselves, treat homeowners equally, and follow due process. When a director crosses the line into harassment, a properly drafted demand letter can stop the behavior, preserve your rights, and create a paper trail for litigation or a restraining order. California courts take board misconduct seriously, and homeowners who document violations early often recover damages, attorney's fees, and injunctive relief. This page explains your rights and how a demand letter works.
lawExplanation: California's Davis-Stirling Act (Civil Code §§ 4000-6150) governs every common interest development in the state and imposes fiduciary duties on HOA board members. Under Corporations Code § 7231(a), a director must act in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation, and with the care, including reasonable inquiry, of an ordinarily prudent person in a like position. Selective enforcement of CC&Rs, retaliation for speaking at meetings, and personal attacks are difficult to reconcile with that standard. Civil Code § 4515 provides that the governing documents may not prohibit a member or resident from peacefully assembling, inviting public officials, canvassing and petitioning, distributing information about association issues, or using social media to discuss association issues, even if critical of the association, and it prohibits retaliation for exercising those rights (§ 4515(e)). A member or resident who is prevented from exercising those rights may bring a civil or small claims action to enjoin enforcement of the offending governing document, and the court may assess a civil penalty of not more than $500 for each violation (§ 4515(d)). Civil Code § 4955 provides that a member who prevails in an action to enforce the open-meeting article is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, and the court may impose a civil penalty of up to $500 per violation; election violations are enforced under § 5145 and record inspection violations under § 5235. If a board member's conduct includes credible threats, stalking, or repeated unwanted contact, California Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6 allows a homeowner to seek a Civil Harassment Restraining Order, which can prohibit contact and require the board member to stay away from your home. Additionally, Civil Code § 5905 requires an association to provide a fair, reasonable, and expeditious procedure for resolving disputes with a member, and under § 5910 a member may invoke it in writing, the association must participate, and the member cannot be charged a fee to participate. Under Civil Code § 5930, an association or a member generally may not file an enforcement action in superior court solely for declaratory, injunctive, or writ relief (or with limited damages) unless the parties have endeavored to submit the dispute to alternative dispute resolution (ADR); the process starts with a Request for Resolution (§ 5935), the other side has 30 days to accept, and the plaintiff files a certificate of compliance (§ 5950). The requirement does not apply to small claims actions or, generally, to assessment disputes. Board members who use HOA resources to harass an owner may also face personal liability for breach of fiduciary duty, defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and violation of the Bane Act (Civil Code § 52.1) if threats or coercion are involved. Documentation of every incident, including dates, witnesses, emails, and meeting minutes, is critical to any successful claim.
letterStrategy: A well-crafted demand letter is often the fastest way to stop harassment from a California HOA board member. The letter should identify the specific board member by name, describe each incident of harassment with dates and witnesses, and cite the exact Davis-Stirling provisions and fiduciary duties being violated. Reference Civil Code § 4515 if your free speech or assembly rights have been chilled, § 4955 if the board violated the open-meeting rules, and Corporations Code § 7231 for the director standard of care. The letter should demand that the harassment cease immediately, that the board member recuse from any matter involving you, and that the association open an investigation under its Code of Conduct. Request dispute resolution under Civil Code § 5910 and put the association on notice that, before any enforcement action for declaratory or injunctive relief, you will endeavor to submit the dispute to ADR under § 5930. Include a clear deadline, typically 30 days, and warn that continued conduct will result in a lawsuit for damages, statutory penalties, attorney's fees, and a civil harassment restraining order under CCP § 527.6. Send the letter by certified mail with return receipt to the board member personally, the HOA's registered agent, and the management company. Keep copies of everything. A strong, statute-specific letter signals that you understand your rights, often prompting the association's insurance carrier and counsel to intervene and rein in the offending director before the dispute escalates.
proceduralNotes: California small claims court has jurisdiction up to $12,500 for individual plaintiffs and is a viable venue for damages claims against an HOA or board member. Filing fees range from $30 to $75 depending on claim size. Civil harassment restraining orders under CCP § 527.6 are filed in superior court with no filing fee for harassment involving violence or threats, and hearings occur within 21-25 days. Before filing an enforcement action in superior court solely for declaratory, injunctive, or writ relief, Civil Code § 5930 requires the parties to endeavor to submit the dispute to ADR, and the plaintiff files a certificate of compliance under § 5950. The statute of limitations is generally two years for personal injury and harassment-related torts and four years for written contract or governing document violations. Prevailing party attorney's fees are available under Civil Code § 5975(c).

faq.q: What counts as harassment by an HOA board member in California?
faq.a: Harassment can include selective enforcement of rules against you, retaliation for speaking at meetings or running for the board, repeated unwanted contact, threats, intimidation, defamation, filing false complaints, restricting your access to common areas, or interfering with your free speech rights under Civil Code § 4515. A single serious incident or a pattern of smaller incidents may qualify. Conduct that would alarm, annoy, or harass a reasonable person, especially when it serves no legitimate HOA purpose, can support both a demand letter and a civil harassment restraining order.

faq.q: Can I sue an individual board member personally, or only the HOA?
faq.a: Yes, California law allows you to sue a board member personally when they act outside the scope of their duties or breach their fiduciary obligations. While the business judgment rule and Corporations Code § 7231.5 protect good-faith decisions, harassment, defamation, intentional misconduct, and personal vendettas are not protected. The HOA's D&O insurance may still apply, but the director can be named individually. Suing personally often motivates faster resolution because the director, not just the association, faces real exposure to damages and attorney's fees.

faq.q: Do I have to use Internal Dispute Resolution before filing a lawsuit?
faq.a: California Civil Code § 5905 requires an association to provide a fair, reasonable, and expeditious procedure for resolving disputes with a member, and under § 5910 a member may invoke it in writing, the association must participate, and the member cannot be charged a fee to participate. Under § 5930, you must generally endeavor to submit the dispute to ADR before filing an enforcement action in superior court for declaratory, injunctive, or writ relief. You must serve a Request for Resolution and wait at least 30 days for a response. However, IDR and ADR are not required before seeking a civil harassment restraining order under CCP § 527.6 or filing in small claims court. A demand letter often satisfies the spirit of these requirements while preserving your options.

faq.q: What damages and penalties can I recover?
faq.a: You can recover actual damages such as emotional distress, lost property value, and out-of-pocket costs. Civil Code § 4955 allows a civil penalty of up to $500 per violation of the open-meeting article. Civil Code § 4515(d) authorizes an action to enjoin a governing document that violates free speech and assembly rights and a civil penalty of up to $500 per violation. Under Civil Code § 5975(c), the prevailing party in an action to enforce governing documents recovers reasonable attorney's fees and costs. If a Bane Act violation is proven, you may recover treble damages plus a statutory penalty of $25,000.

faq.q: How long do I have to take action against a harassing board member?
faq.a: California's statute of limitations depends on the claim. Personal injury and emotional distress claims generally must be filed within two years under Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1. Defamation claims have a one-year limit under § 340(c). An action for violation of a recorded restriction has a five-year limit under § 336(b), and an action on a written contract has a four-year limit under § 337. Sending a demand letter early preserves evidence, creates a clear record, and often resolves the dispute well before any limitations period becomes a concern.
